subject: History of USA
title: 5. The Constitution of the United States

segments.text: Federalism and separation of powers are frequently confused — federalism divides authority between national and state governments (a vertical division), while separation of powers divides authority among the three federal branches (a horizontal division). Keeping these precisely distinct is the topic’s single highest-value point.
The Constitution divides authority between the national government (enumerated and implied powers) and the states (broad retained authority, subject to constitutional limits).

creates an independently elected executive with powers including command of the armed forces, treaty negotiation and appointments — though many actions require congressional funding or Senate approval, meaning executive power is constitutionally shared, not isolated.

blocks.text: Judiciary, Checks and Balances, and Amendment

segments.text: creates the Supreme Court and authorises lower federal courts;

, allowing courts to invalidate unconstitutional government action — importantly, this power is not written in one explicit constitutional sentence but developed through interpretation and precedent. Vetoes, overrides, impeachment, confirmation, appropriations and judicial review force the branches to share and contest power continuously — separation of powers means controlled interaction, not total isolation.

requires supermajorities for amendment, making constitutional change difficult but possible; amendments have abolished slavery, expanded voting rights, and altered presidential and electoral procedures over time.

items.text: The power of federal courts to invalidate unconstitutional government action, established through practice (Marbury v. Madison, 1803) rather than explicit constitutional text.
Federalism = national-state division (vertical); separation of powers = division among federal branches (horizontal) — never merge these two concepts.
Read the Constitution itself; create a branch table (selection, term, major powers, checks on other branches); make a separate federal-versus-state powers sheet.
Do not confuse federalism with separation of powers.
Do not say judicial review is written in one explicit constitutional sentence; it developed through interpretation and practice.
Do not treat the Constitution as unchanged since 1787; amendments and judicial doctrine have significantly altered its operation.
The Constitution was signed in 1787; the federal government began operating in 1789.
Legislative power is vested in a bicameral Congress (House and Senate); executive power in the president; judicial power in the Supreme Court and lower federal courts.
Amendments require special supermajority procedures under Article V.
Keep federalism (national-state) and separation of powers (among federal branches) precisely distinct — this single distinction resolves most confusion on this topic.
Judicial review is a developed constitutional practice, not an explicit textual grant — an important nuance for any strong constitutional-law answer.
